blocks.text: Code written against a supertype must keep working, unchanged, when handed any subtype.

Liskov's rule concerns **behavioral** compatibility, not signatures. A subtype may weaken preconditions and strengthen postconditions and invariants, never the reverse, and must not allow state changes the supertype forbids. Substitutability is judged by what clients **rely on**, which is why real-world 'is-a' is a poor guide.

items: **Preconditions:** a subtype may accept more, never less.
**Postconditions and invariants:** may promise more, never less.
**History:** no new state transitions the supertype disallows.

blocks.text: The compiler checks signatures only. LSP violations compile cleanly and surface later as `instanceof` checks, thrown `UnsupportedOperationException` or wrong results.

walkthrough.note: A mutable `Square` extends `Rect` and keeps its sides equal. It compiles, and geometry says it is a rectangle.
`stretch` relies on a contract the supertype implies: setting width and height independently gives `5 * 2`.
Substitutability is restored by removing mutation. Both shapes are immutable records behind a sealed `Shape` that promises only `area()`.

blocks.text: A payment gateway where one method cannot refund.

A `PaymentMethod` interface had `charge` and `refund`. A `GiftCard` implementation threw on `refund`, and the nightly reconciliation job, which reverses failed orders through the same interface, crashed. The fix was not a `try/catch` in the job. Refund moved to a `Refundable` sub-interface, so the job's signature states exactly what it can rely on.

lines: void reverse(Order o, Refundable method) { method.refund(o.receipt()); }

blocks.text: Payoff: the unsupported case becomes a compile error instead of a 3 a.m. exception.

lists.title: Use when
items: Designing an abstract type that third parties will implement.
Reviewing a subclass that overrides a method to throw, no-op or narrow its inputs.
Writing contract tests every implementation must pass.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: Using inheritance as taxonomy: a square "is a" rectangle only in geometry.
Patching a violation with `instanceof` in the client.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Overrides that throw `UnsupportedOperationException` for an inherited method.
A subclass rejecting inputs the parent accepted, such as `null`.
Mutable subtypes breaking an invariant clients assumed.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Records and sealed interfaces remove most of the mutation that causes LSP breaks.
`equals`, `hashCode` and `compareTo` have contracts that every override must honor.

rows.difference: Fat interfaces force implementers to stub methods and thereby break substitutability; narrow roles prevent it.
Composition avoids the subtype relationship altogether, so there is no supertype contract to violate.
OCP extends through new subtypes; LSP is what keeps those extensions safe for existing clients.
Immutability removes the history-rule violations that make mutable subtypes unsafe.

entries.name: List.of / Collections.unmodifiableList
entries.detail: `add` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`: the JDK documents these as optional operations, a known compromise.

entries.name: Object.equals and Comparable.compareTo
entries.detail: Their documented contracts (symmetry, transitivity, consistency) are LSP rules every subclass must keep.

entries.name: java.util.Properties
entries.detail: Extends `Hashtable<Object,Object>`, so callers can insert non-`String` entries that `getProperty` ignores.

entries.name: java.util.Stack
entries.detail: Extends `Vector`, so a stack can be indexed and inserted into at any position, violating stack discipline.

exercises.prompt: Which principle does this subclass break?
lines: // callers elsewhere: store.write(report); String s = store.read();

options.why: Callers of `FileStore` expect `write` to work; the subtype refuses a promise of its supertype.
Splitting read and write would be the remedy, but the violation is the subtype breaking the contract.
Nothing was edited in the base class; the extension itself is the problem.
No concrete dependency is hard-wired anywhere in this code.

template: class FileStore { String read() { return ""; } void write(String d) {} }

exercises.scenario: A `Queue` interface documents FIFO order. A teammate adds `PriorityQueueAdapter` implementing it so the scheduler can use it. All unit tests pass, but an ordering-sensitive job produces wrong results in production.

options.why: The adapter satisfies the signatures but not the documented FIFO contract that clients rely on.
Extending without edits is what OCP wants; the issue is that the extension is not substitutable.
The scheduler depends on an abstraction already; the abstraction was not honored.
The interface is not too wide; one implementation breaks its promises.

exercises.prompt: Tap the line that makes the subtype unsubstitutable.
lines: void increment() { value++; }   // value() grows by one
exercises.explanation: `CappedCounter` silently ignores `increment()`, so code expecting `value()` to grow by one breaks. Do not extend `Counter` for a bounded variant; model it as a separate type or put the cap in the base contract.

exercises.prompt: Order the contract check so that each step only uses what came before.
exercises.explanation: Obtain the object through the supertype, mutate it, read the derived value, then check the contract. Each step consumes the previous result.

template: class Rect { int w, h; void setW(int w) { this.w = w; } void setH(int h) { this.h = h; } int area() { return w * h; } }

exercises.prompt: State the Liskov Substitution Principle in your own words and explain why a mutable `Square extends Rectangle` breaks it.

modelAnswer.text: Any code written for a supertype must work with any subtype without knowing which. It is about behavior, not signatures: preconditions cannot tighten, postconditions cannot weaken. A mutable Square couples width and height, so code that sets them independently and expects the product gets the wrong area.

keyPoints: Substitutability is behavioral, not just type-level
Preconditions cannot tighten; postconditions cannot weaken
Mutable Square breaks the independent width/height expectation
Fix by redesigning: immutability, composition or narrower interfaces
